title: How to Set Up an Ad Spy Watchlist Before You Enter a New Niche
excerpt: An ad spy watchlist turns scattered competitor ads into a weekly signal. This setup covers which advertisers to track, which fields to log, and how repeats become test briefs.
body: Ad spy tools are good at volume and bad at judgment. You can pull hundreds of competitor creatives in an afternoon and still not know whether a niche is worth entering. A watchlist fixes that by turning a firehose into a weekly signal. Instead of browsing, you track a small fixed set of advertisers, log the same fields every week, and let repetition tell you what is working. It takes about twenty minutes a week and it replaces the expensive habit of copying whatever creative appeared most recently.

Choose eight to twelve advertisers, not a hundred. The right ones have been running paid ads for at least three weeks, have published more than one creative, and sell in the price band you plan to sell in. Three weeks of continuous spend is the cheapest available proof that an offer converts, because nobody keeps an unprofitable ad alive that long on purpose. Drop any advertiser that disappears within a week and replace it. A watchlist that keeps its size is a watchlist you will actually maintain.

Log the same fields for every new creative you see. The hook in the first three seconds, the offer, the price shown, the format, whether the landing page is a product page or a collection, and how many days the ad has been running. Keep it in one sheet with one row per creative and let it grow. Six weeks in, patterns you would never spot by browsing become obvious: hooks that repeat across advertisers, price points that hold, and formats that quietly stop appearing. Those patterns are the real output.

Run a short weekly review with three buckets. Repeat patterns go into the test bucket, because something several advertisers share is a convention of the niche rather than one brand's taste. New angles go into the watch bucket and stay there until a second advertiser copies them. Price moves go into a note to yourself, because a competitor discounting tells you about their margin, not about whether you should discount. Do not act on a single creative, however good it looks. One ad is a test someone else is running.

Turn the test bucket into three briefs a month, each with one variable. If every advertiser leads with a demonstration, your variable is the demonstration and you hold the offer constant. If every advertiser leads with price, your variable is the framing of that price. Write the brief before you open the ad manager, including the metric that decides it and the spend cap that ends it. A brief with a pre committed stopping rule costs less and teaches more than a campaign you keep extending because it is nearly working.

Watch for saturation. When watchlist advertisers run nearly identical hooks, when new entrants appear every week, and when the average ad lifespan drops, the niche is getting crowded and the same result will cost you more creative spend. That is a decision point rather than a disaster: differentiate on product, differentiate on offer, or pick another niche while your costs are still small. The DTCwise Ad Spy category at /category/ad-spy keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing, and /tool/bigspy is where most of this tracking starts.
